passage: Last year my photo page looked perfect: the debate trophy, the beach trip, the new haircut. I spent twenty minutes on every caption. People left hearts under everything, and I, Yamini, still ate lunch pretending to text so nobody would notice I had nobody to talk to. I was scared that if anyone saw how often I doubted myself, they'd leave. Then in March, Vaibhav from my bus stop asked why a girl with such a perfect page never looked happy in person. I almost said, "I'm fine." Instead I said, "I don't know who I am when I'm not performing." He didn't laugh. He said he felt the same about his gym videos. We talk at the bus stop most mornings now. It's only one person. It's more than all those hearts.

qa.q: What did Vaibhav ask Yamini in March?
qa.a: He asked why a girl with such a perfect page never looked happy in person.

qa.q: Why did Yamini pretend to text at lunch?
qa.a: She was afraid people would notice she had nobody to talk to, and worried that showing her doubts would make them leave.

qa.q: What was the turning point for Yamini, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Choosing to say "I don't know who I am when I'm not performing" instead of "I'm fine." One honest answer let a real friendship begin.

qa.q: What might Vaibhav have gained from Yamini's honest reply?
qa.a: It gave him room to admit he felt the same about his gym videos, so he didn't have to feel alone either.

grounding: A teenager hides doubts behind a polished online self, feels alone among many followers, and one real disclosure starts to change that.

passage:
Counsellor's note, Class 10. Parveen.
Imran (15) came in to "ask about streams" and spent ten minutes on marks. Classmates see him as the funny one, and his short videos get big numbers. Near the end, looking at the floor, he said, "Everyone knows me and nobody knows me." He told me he deletes any post where he looks tired or unsure. I thanked him for telling me, said many students feel this and it isn't a weakness, and asked if there was one person he'd trust with one small true thing. He named his cousin Faiz. Plan: he will tell Faiz one honest thing this week. I'll check in with him at lunch on Wednesday, and we meet again on Friday.

qa.q: What did Imran say he deletes?
qa.a: Any post where he looks tired or unsure.

qa.q: What does Imran looking at the floor while saying "Everyone knows me and nobody knows me" suggest?
qa.a: He feels lonely behind his funny image and is nervous about admitting it, as if afraid of being judged.

qa.q: Why was asking Imran to share one small true thing with Faiz a good step?
qa.a: It keeps the risk small, so he can test whether honesty brings rejection or closeness, with the counsellor checking in along the way.

qa.q: How might Faiz be affected if Imran shares something honest?
qa.a: Faiz may feel trusted and closer to Imran, and might open up in return 🙂

grounding: A teenager who shows a polished, funny self feels unknown and alone, and a counsellor helps him take a first small step toward real disclosure.

Thursday, 10:40 pm
The class group was full of Samir's birthday pics tonight. I'm in six of them, laughing. Nobody would guess I spent half the party in the washroom because I felt like a fake.
I keep a version of me for them: chill, good at football, never stressed. The real one is scared of failing the maths re-test and thinks nobody would stay if they saw him.
But on the walk home Samir asked, "Bro, you okay? You went missing." And I said... actually, no. Told him about the re-test. He said he failed chemistry last term and hid it too!!
Didn't expect that. Feel lighter. Also weird. Going to sleep.
Kunal

passage:
Everyone at the tuition centre near the Jorhat tea estate knew Bhupen, fifteen: the boy who did impressions of the sir, always had a joke and never seemed to study. On the bus home the back seat crowded around him.
He never mentioned that his mother had gone to work in Bengaluru in March, or that he cooked rice for his little brother every night and fell asleep over his books. When the others talked about their mothers' cooking, he cracked a joke and looked out of the window.
One evening the bus broke down and only Alka was left at the stand with him. "You're funny," she said, "but you always look tired." He almost laughed it off. Then he told her about the rice, and his mother's voice on the phone. Alka didn't say much. "My father works away too." They waited in silence, and it felt less lonely than the crowded back seat.

qa.q: Where had Bhupen's mother gone to work in March?
qa.a: She had gone to work in Bengaluru.

qa.q: Why did Bhupen crack a joke and look out of the window when others talked about their mothers' cooking?
qa.a: He was hiding how much he missed his mother, afraid that showing it would change how the others saw him.

qa.q: At the bus stand, what did Bhupen choose instead of laughing it off, and what did it change?
qa.a: He told Alka about cooking rice and his mother's calls, and that honest moment felt less lonely than the crowded back seat.

qa.q: What might it mean to Alka that Bhupen trusted her with this?
qa.a: Alka might feel trusted and understood, since her own father works away too.

grounding: A popular, joking teenager hides his loneliness at home, feels alone in the crowd, and begins to change it through one honest disclosure.

passage: Every photo Vera posted from Lyon looked the same: perfect croissant, perfect bike ride, a caption with three sparkles. Two hundred likes, forty comments. At lunch the table laughed at her jokes, and she laughed with them, and walked home alone. Nobody knew she had failed the chemistry mock twice or that she lay awake doubting she'd get into any programme at all. Telling felt risky, like people would see the cracks and leave. On Friday the tram broke down, and she ended up waiting beside Tariq, the quiet boy from physics. "You always look like you've got it sorted," he said. Vera almost laughed it off. Instead she heard herself say, "I failed chem. Twice." Tariq blinked. "Same. Well, maths." They talked for forty minutes, and it was the first time in months her chest felt loose.

qa.q: How many times did Vera fail the chemistry mock?
qa.a: She failed the chemistry mock twice.

qa.q: Why was Vera afraid to tell anyone about her doubts?
qa.a: She feared that if people saw the cracks, they would leave, so she felt safer hiding behind a perfect image even though it left her lonely.

qa.q: What small step helped Vera feel less alone?
qa.a: Choosing to answer Tariq honestly instead of laughing it off opened a real conversation, showing that one true disclosure can start closeness.

qa.q: How might Tariq have seen Vera before and after the tram stop?
qa.a: Before, Tariq saw someone who looked sorted and out of reach; afterwards he likely felt relieved to learn she struggled too, just as he did.

grounding: A teenager who shows a polished self and hides doubts feels alone among many, until a real disclosure begins to change that.

passage: The robotics lab at Kendriya School smelled of solder and old chalk. Gopika was team lead, the girl who always knew the answer, whose reels of the line-follower bot got shared by juniors. Nobody saw her rewire the same board at eleven at night, sure she was a fraud who'd been lucky. At lunch she sat with six people and felt like she was behind glass. On Wednesday the bot died again two days before the district round. Hemant, who handled the code, found her staring at it. "Should I tell Sir we're behind?" he asked. Gopika's throat tightened. "Hemant, I don't actually know what's wrong. I haven't for a week." He put down his laptop. "I thought I was the only one faking it." They laughed shakily, pulled up a stool each, and started over from the battery.

qa.q: How many days before the district round did the bot die again?
qa.a: The bot died again two days before the district round.

qa.q: What was Gopika feeling at lunch, sitting with six people?
qa.a: Gopika felt lonely and cut off, as if she were behind glass, because nobody knew her doubts.

qa.q: What went right when Gopika told Hemant the truth?
qa.a: Her honesty let Hemant admit his own doubts, so they could work on the real problem together instead of both pretending.

qa.q: How did Gopika's confession affect Hemant?
qa.a: Hemant seemed relieved, because he had thought he was the only one faking it and now felt less alone.

grounding: A teenager keeps up a polished, capable image while hiding doubts, feels alone among many, and a real disclosure begins to ease it.

passage:

Nikita

passage:
"You asked what my life is really like. I'm Vijay, sixteen. Online, I'm the funny one. Perfect photos, jokes in every group chat, two thousand followers.
In real life I lie awake worrying about my marks and my parents' fights. I've never told anyone. Not even my best friend, Usha.
I think if people see the real me, they'll leave. So I keep the jokes going. Everyone thinks I'm fine. I'm surrounded all day and still lonely.
Last week Usha asked, 'Are you okay? You seem tired.' I almost said the usual. But I said, 'Not really.' She didn't leave. She just asked, 'Want to talk?'
It was the first real thing I've said in months. I'm scared. But it felt lighter."

passage:

October: At a sleepover, Karthik admitted he was scared about his parents' job losses. Siddharth almost said something too. Instead he made a joke. Later, lying awake, he felt more alone than ever.
December: Walking home, Karthik said, "You never tell me anything real." Siddharth stopped. "Maths is killing me. And at home I feel invisible." Karthik nodded. "Thanks for telling me." Siddharth felt his shoulders drop for the first time in weeks.

qa.q: Who arrived at Siddharth's home?
qa.a: His baby sister arrived.

qa.q: What did Siddharth feel lying awake after the sleepover?

qa.q: What changed in December, and why did it help?
qa.a: Siddharth told Karthik the truth about maths and feeling invisible; the real disclosure brought relief and closeness.

qa.q: How might Karthik feel when Siddharth finally opens up?
qa.a: Karthik probably feels trusted and closer, especially after sharing his own fears earlier.

passage: Everyone in Class 10B thought Binita had it together: glossy notes, a hundred friends, a laugh you could hear across the Bhubaneswar school grounds. At Shreya's birthday party she laughed at every joke and danced first. Then she slipped away to the balcony and stared at the traffic for twenty minutes. Shreya found her there. 'Party's too boring for you?' 'No, it's great.' A long pause. Binita's smile stayed on, and then it slipped. 'I'm so tired of being Binita. If people knew how scared I am of the boards, and that I cry after every test, they'd think I'm fake.' Shreya sat on the railing beside her. 'I cry after tests too. I thought you were the one person who didn't.' They laughed, shakily, and stayed out till the cake came.

qa.q: Where did Binita slip away to?
qa.a: To the balcony.

qa.q: What does Binita's smile slipping suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Binita was exhausted and lonely behind the polished self, scared people would see her as fake.

qa.q: What could help Binita feel less alone from here?
qa.a: Sharing honestly with a few trusted people like Shreya, and perhaps talking to the school counsellor about exam stress.

qa.q: How does Shreya's view of Binita change?
qa.a: Shreya had seen Binita as the one person who never cried after tests, and now sees she is not alone in her own fear.

'Nice post,' Dhruv said, sliding his phone across the canteen table. 'Five hundred likes for a sunset.'
'Five hundred and twelve,' Anirban said, grinning.
'You looked so happy in the pic.'
'I was.'
'You were panicking about the physics test five minutes before. I was there.'
Anirban's grin stayed, but he started folding his napkin into smaller and smaller squares. 'So?'
'So I don't know which you is real sometimes.'
'That's the point, na. Nobody wants the real one.'
'I might.'
Anirban stopped folding. 'I'm not sure about anything right now. Marks, college, what I'm even good at.' He looked up fast. 'Don't make it a thing.'
'Not a thing,' Dhruv said. 'Eat your samosa. Then tell me more.'

qa.q: How many likes did the sunset post get?
qa.a: Five hundred and twelve.

qa.q: What does Anirban's napkin-folding suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Anirban felt uneasy and exposed when Dhruv pointed out the gap between the post and reality.

qa.q: What did Dhruv do well in responding?
qa.a: He noticed gently, said he might want the real Anirban, and kept it low-key, so Anirban felt safe enough to share more.

qa.q: What is it like for Dhruv to see the gap between the post and the real Anirban?
qa.a: Dhruv feels unsure which Anirban is real and wants to be let in, not just shown the happy picture.

I felt surrounded and completely by myself. On the last night, on the terrace, with the crackers mostly done, Saurabh said his parents had been fighting a lot. He said it quietly, like it cost him. So I told him about chemistry. Nothing broke. He just nodded and said, "Same boat, different leak." Then Ammi called up, "Asif beta, come down, food!" and I went downstairs lighter than I'd been all week.
